title: Why Levels Matter in the Language Classroom
brief: Explain why identifying a learner's proficiency level is a practical necessity for the classroom teacher, not an administrative formality. Cover how mismatched level placement leads to concrete problems — material that is too easy produces boredom and disengagement, while material that is too difficult produces anxiety and silence. Use invented classroom examples (e.g., a beginner handed a newspaper article, an advanced learner drilled on 'Hello, my name is…') to make the point vivid. Establish that levels give teachers a shared vocabulary for planning, grouping, and selecting tasks, and that this unit introduces two complementary frameworks for thinking about level: the traditional band system used widely in language schools and the CEFR scale used internationally.

title: The Traditional Band System: Six Levels at a Glance
brief: Introduce the six traditional proficiency bands — beginner, elementary, pre-intermediate, intermediate, upper-intermediate, and advanced — as the everyday working vocabulary of most language schools and TEFL courses. Briefly characterise each band in terms of what a learner at that stage can typically do with English: for example, a beginner can manage only isolated words and memorised phrases, while an upper-intermediate learner can handle most everyday topics with only occasional errors. Keep descriptions concise here, since the following section expands on each level in detail. Note that these labels are not perfectly standardized across every school or publisher, so teachers should treat them as approximate guides rather than rigid categories, and that the bands map loosely onto the CEFR scale introduced later in the unit.

title: Inside Each Level: What Learners Can Typically Do
brief: Provide a fuller, level-by-level breakdown of learner ability across the six traditional bands, focusing on what this means for classroom planning. For each level, describe typical vocabulary range, grammatical control, and communicative ability using invented examples: for instance, an elementary learner can ask 'Where is the station?' but struggles to explain why they are late, while an intermediate learner can narrate a past event but may still confuse the present perfect and simple past. Show how these differences directly shape lesson choices — task complexity, the amount of teacher talk, how much scaffolding is needed, and what error correction is appropriate. This section should be the most detailed in the unit and give trainee teachers a practical mental picture of each level.

title: The CEFR Scale: A Common International Reference
brief: Introduce the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) as a widely used international framework that organises proficiency into six levels: A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, and C2, grouped into three broad bands — Basic User (A), Independent User (B), and Proficient User (C). Explain in plain, original language what a learner at each level can broadly do: for example, an A1 learner can introduce themselves and answer simple questions about personal details, while a C2 learner can understand virtually everything they hear or read and express themselves with precision and nuance. Do not reproduce any official descriptor text; all descriptions must be the writer's own words. Explain that the CEFR levels map onto the traditional bands (e.g., A1–A2 corresponds roughly to beginner–elementary, B1–B2 to pre-intermediate–upper-intermediate, C1–C2 to advanced and beyond), giving teachers a bridge between the two systems.

title: How Level Shapes Lesson Planning Decisions
brief: Show how a teacher's knowledge of learner level translates into concrete planning choices, drawing on the level descriptions established in the previous sections. Cover at least four planning dimensions: choice of text or input (e.g., a picture story for A1 versus an opinion article for B2), language focus (e.g., present simple and basic vocabulary at beginner level versus conditionals and collocation at upper-intermediate), task design (controlled drills versus open discussion), and the degree of support or scaffolding provided. Use invented classroom scenarios to illustrate contrasts — for example, how the same topic of 'travel' would be handled very differently with an A2 class and a C1 class. Reinforce the idea that level awareness is not about limiting learners but about pitching input and tasks in the zone where learning can actually happen.

title: Mixed-Level Classes and Reading the Room
brief: Address the reality that many real-world classes contain learners at different points on the proficiency scale — a common situation in private language schools, community programmes, and company training. Explain practical strategies a teacher can use: differentiated tasks (giving the same topic but different texts or different output expectations to different learners), open-ended activities that allow multiple entry points, and strategic pairing of stronger and weaker learners for collaborative work. Use invented examples, such as a class where some learners can write a full paragraph while others can only produce a few sentences on the same prompt. Close the section by reminding trainee teachers that level is not fixed — learners move through the bands over time — and that regularly reassessing where learners are is part of responsive, professional teaching.
